To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of long call sequences recorded by automatic acoustic recording units is necessary to assess the within-individual call variation of a species.

the intra-individual variation in acoustic signals is underestimated by the use of short recording sessions and that the use of 3 short and evenly-distributed recording sessions is sufficient to capture most of the signal variability.
the intra-individual variation of the dominant frequency in tree frog advertisement calls can be estimated using short and well-differentiated recordings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of the intra-individual variability of acoustic signals and with the design of sampling methods to capture this variability in the field.
the estimation of signal variability at various scales (individual, population and species).
the use of automatic acoustic recording units to study sexual selection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of automatic recording units should be recommended to estimate signal variability in natural conditions, but that the use of a few short and well-distribuited records should be preferred to estimate the nightly signal variability of a given male.
the call dominant frequency is a good indicator of the male quality, but only when it is measured with a sufficient number of calls and at the right time of the calling period.

the call dominant frequency variation in H. arbora is high, that this variation is not captured by the current automatic recording units (which are not adapted to this type of study), and that it would be necessary to adapt them to capture this type of information.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the purpose of studying the intra-individual variability in the acoustic signals of treefrogs, the use of automatic recorders is a good option.
, to assess intra-individual signal variability, the best method is to record a few calls at different time during the night.
the assessment of signal variability is a crucial issue in the study of signal function and the use of long recordings will be necessary to get accurate results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is necessary to use a sufficient number of calls and a sufficient time sampling to capture the nightly variability of acoustic signals.
the use of short records (2 to 3 minutes) distributed over time (beginning, end and middle of the night in our case) is the best way to estimate signal variability.
the use of automatic recording units should be accompanied by the development of new methods for the analysis of the long call sequences that they produce.
